- the agenda calls for the statements by the council and the commission on the preparation of the thessaloniki european council of 20 and 21 june 2003 and the meeting of the troika and the countries participating in the stability pact for south-east europe.
council mr president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, the thessaloniki council is coming to end a particularly difficult six-month period and to pave the way for the continuation of the european integration process. the council is expected to focus on five major modules. firstly, how to proceed with the institutional changes needed by the european union, which have been being worked on since march 2002 by the convention on the future of europe. secondly, foreign and defence policy, with particular emphasis on the transatlantic relations, the development of a strategic approach to union security and weapons of mass destruction. thirdly, the issues of immigration, asylum and external borders, which you know are of interest to the greek presidency and have become increasingly important to the union in recent years. the council will be dealing with the employment strategy and the lisbon strategy in general, and a fifth section will be devoted to the union's policy in the western balkans on the following day, saturday 21 june. the council will of course be discussing and taking appropriate decisions on a number of other subjects besides these five main subjects. i would like to make a few comments on the commission's proposal. the first part of the report, ladies and gentlemen, concerns the institutional changes which the assembly is considering and the steps which must be taken. the enlargement, the treaty of which was signed in athens on 16 april, raises the urgent problem of the changes that must be made if the european union is not to fall into the ugly trap of rigidity, of the inability of its institutions and bodies to function effectively and creatively. the future of europe is a matter for the council and the union in general. as agreed at the informal council in april, the assembly, through its president, is expected to present the results of its work, which has lasted some 15 months. the greek presidency, after special and multiple consultations, ensured that the timetable given to the assembly by the copenhagen council was respected. ideas and proposals have been submitted. the debate can go on, but at some point we have to end it. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the final product of the convention will therefore be presented to the council of thessaloniki. the role of the council is not to take decisions on the substance, its role is to decide how to instruct the intergovernmental conference to start work so that we can have a result that will be acceptable to all, that will be a common denominator and will constitute the institutional framework that will determine the course of the union for several years. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. the greek presidency looks forward to a debate on the substance of the issues, in order to exchange views, to form an image of the national positions before the intergovernmental conference and, of course, to take decisions on procedural matters concerning the continuation of the procedure. the timetable for the work of the intergovernmental conference is an important issue. the timetable should also take into account the obligation of some member states to hold an internal dialogue on the outcome of the convention. we estimate that this process should be completed by the autumn, the intergovernmental conference should be in place and its work should be completed in time so that the period between the date of enlargement in may 2004 and the entry into force of the new institutional system is as short as possible. the progress of the work in the assembly does, however, allow me to express certain views on a number of points. the debate on the institutional architecture of the enlarged union began with the need for greater efficiency. it is the common conviction that we must adapt the institutional structure and functioning to the needs of a larger union, while maintaining the principles on which the european project of unification is based. the drafting of a constitutional treaty is a major qualitative leap, largely due to the efforts made by the assembly. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the strength of the european union will be based on two key elements: a more democratic functioning and more effective decision-making. i would particularly like to welcome the fact that the work of the assembly has shown a considerable degree of consensus on a number of key issues, such as the strengthening of the role of the european parliament, the establishment of the union's single international legal personality, the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into the constitutional treaty and the further communicalization of the area of freedom, security and justice. it is also widely accepted that we can achieve greater democratic legitimacy in the union without creating new institutions or bodies. the enlarged union should also lead to a strong international presence. this requires finding solutions, such as a more coordinated use of foreign policy instruments and the creation of a person who will combine the responsibilities of the high representative with those of the commissioner responsible for foreign policy. as you know, ladies and gentlemen, this debate is ongoing. in addition to the different approaches expressed in the plenary of the assembly, i think it is important to ensure a balance between the union's institutions, to preserve the equality of the member states, to further exploit the advantages of the community method and to strengthen the democratic character of a union of states and peoples. in any event, i consider that the assembly has been successful in reaching decisions on a number of difficult issues that were outstanding from previous intergovernmental conferences. it goes without saying that the forthcoming intergovernmental conference will have to take account of decisions reached by consensus, and it is important that in the final phase of the work there should be a spirit of compromise, that the prestige of the convention should be preserved and that a strong result be secured, which the union so badly needs. as i said, a second important area of work at the june council was related to developments over this period in the highly sensitive area of foreign policy, which includes the question of intergovernmental relations. the union and the united states will hold a summit in washington a few days after the council. it is an opportunity to discuss issues of importance to both sides, to work together to tackle serious issues of concern to international and bilateral developments and to reverse the climate that has often prevailed in recent months. the european union and the united states are based on traditional ties, the two sides' weighty international role and their dynamic, although in recent months they have been tested by differences of opinion on a number of issues. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. at the last meeting of the gimnich we had a very useful discussion. we believe that the picture of our relations with the united states should be improved and better reflect the real state of our relations. to this end, we are working particularly hard to ensure that the next summit, the issues of which will be discussed at the thessaloniki summit, will be an important step in further developing our strategic relationship to address together the challenges of our times. the issues of iraq, transatlantic relations and international developments in general have recently created new challenges for the field of european security and defence policy. in this area, we should be able to develop a common understanding of the new security environment and be able to respond effectively to new challenges and threats. at their informal meeting in early may, the foreign ministers instructed the high representative of the union to prepare a general report on the new security environment, the challenges and threats arising from it and ways in which the union could deal with them, to be presented and discussed for the first time at the thessaloniki european council. the european council is also expected to adopt the presidency's progress report on european security and defence policy and the annual report on the implementation of the union programme on the prevention of violent conflicts, which is a cornerstone of the union's security mechanism. the related issue of weapons of mass destruction is also on the important agenda and i certainly believe it will remain there, as the proliferation of these weapons is a major challenge to the international issue. following the conclusions of the seville european council, the presidency intends to bring to the attention of the heads of state, in the context of the june council, a number of issues of migration, asylum and external borders, which you know were a key priority of our presidency. the progress made is substantial. the council has managed to reach political agreement on the directive on family reunification and we believe that we will be able to reach political agreement on the directive on longterm residents and a co-directive on the definition of refugee. as you know, we have sought to take a holistic view of the issue of immigration in terms of legal and illegal immigration. in the process of formulating a single european policy on legal immigration and asylum, the presidency has also attached particular importance to the integration of third-country nationals. together with the commission we intend to draw conclusions for thessaloniki on the basis of the commission communication on the development of a common policy on illegal immigration, trafficking in human beings, external border issues and the return of illegal immigrants, also in conjunction with the issue of burden sharing. the presidency also intends to seek political agreement to include migration as a necessary parameter in the assessment of third countries' cooperation with the union. following the spring european council, which took place in the context of difficult economic and political developments, it is also necessary to take measures to implement the decisions reached in the framework of the lisbon strategy in march 2000, especially as one third of the way through this process has been completed and much remains to be done. the march council decided to promote the implementation of a series of policies on employment, innovation, 1997 selectivity and the copenhagen criteria. in the spirit of this change, the commission has proposed a specific instrument, the european integration partnerships. inspired by the pre-accession commission. the regulation on general food law, which entered into force in february 2002, contains new provisions as regards the rapid alert system. with a view to increasing transparency according to article 10, the commission published for the first time a report on the rapid alert system for food and feed for the year 2002. we will do so for each subsequent year. however, we cannot apply the food law retroactively and go back as far as 1992. the publication of this annual report was, however, only the first step. in addition, since the end of may 2003, the commission has published, on the internet, summary reports containing information on all notifications received on a weekly basis. these reports contain information on the type of product and the problem identified, the origin of the product and the notifying member state. the rapid alert system defined in article 50 of the regulation is designed primarily as a tool for the rapid transmission of information amongst competent authorities in cases where a risk has been identified and measures have already been taken by the notifying member state, such as withholding, recalling, seizure or rejection of the products concerned. the quick transmission of information allows all other member states to verify immediately whether they are also affected by the problem in question, or to ensure that a product rejected at one point of entry does not enter through another place. it also ensures coherent and simultaneous actions by all member states. in cases where a product is still on the market and should not be consumed, the authorities of the member states are in a position to take all the necessary urgent measures, including providing direct information to the public. in addition, the information collected by the rapid alert system is used by the commission. for example, my services use the information to set priorities for the food and veterinary office and to propose measures such as suspension of the placing on the market, suspension of imports or any other emergency measure under article 53 of the regulation. the commission also uses this information to assist third countries. when products subject to a notification originate from a third country, its competent authorities are systematically informed in order to enable them to correct the problem at source and prevent further cases. it is true that, according to article 52 of the food law regulation, the commission does not publish trade names and the identity of individual companies in the regular rapid alert summaries. however, where emergency measures are taken by member states or the commission, in the light of the analysis of the risk posed by the alert, such relevant information on the products concerned by the action is made public. the rasff is used both to take actions to prevent further occurrence of food-related risks and to react immediately to such related risks in order to provide consumers with safe food.
i would like to thank the commissioner for that information. in relation to trade names and individual companies it is very important that a vague system of alerts is in place which allows the consumer to make a choice. does the commission not agree that if a product or food producer causes an alert then it is both in the consumer's interest and indeed in the interest of the open market that this information should be made public? i would like to ask the commissioner a question concerning the 2002 rapid alerts. apparently, 26% of rapid alerts in 2002 were caused by fish. what is the breakdown of these alerts between farmed fish and wild fish? the consumer has a right to know if farmed fish cause a disproportionate number of rapid alerts. is dg sanco taking any specific action to address this problem? does the commissioner have this information on him now? it would be very useful to have this information on the breakdown as regards fish.
mr president, my group will be supporting a number of the compromise amendments that have been put forward. this must have been very difficult for the rapporteur in face of members of this parliament who want to drag their heels for the benefit of the packaging industry. however, looking at the current packaging directive and at compliance with it, and just looking at my own country ireland and a number of others, for example portugal and greece – they are all now looking for derogations for extra time. in my opinion, they are being rewarded for being tardy and environmentally irresponsible. this is sending out a very dangerous message to the applicant countries. if the existing member states cannot comply with the existing legislation and cannot meet their targets then it is going to be very difficult to argue and to push for the new countries coming in to do the same, since they come from an economically less well-off background. some of the proposals that have been put forward in the legislation were alarming. the idea of a maximum target for recycling is crazy. if member states can recycle 100% then surely they should be allowed to do so and to set a ceiling here is irresponsible. the issue of recovery is a major problem. recovery is stretching definitions to the extreme. recovery is basically a nice term for incineration; it is burning and then producing heat. the idea of a minimum target for recovery will to a certain extent force member states who do not have incineration to bring it in or to use that as an excuse. perhaps the wording is not as bad as it was originally. this is a major problem for countries like ireland that have not done anything about their waste problem. they will say, we are going to recover, and that sounds very nice. at this stage we have to do what has been proposed by some other speakers. we have to eliminate, reduce and recycle, and then finally disposal should be the last option. burning waste and calling it recovery is stretching the imagination to the extreme.
mr president, key to the 1994 directive were targets for member states for packaging recovery and recycling, to be set initially for a five-year phase and thereafter to be reviewed for subsequent five-year phases – and hence we are here today. i support the objective of this directive to minimise the impact of packaging and packaging waste, as long as the costs are proportionate to the environmental benefits. it is often forgotten that packaging waste is only a small proportion of total landfill. the key concern in relation to the amendments to this directive is the deadline for achieving compliance with the proposed higher recovery and recycling targets. the deadline, or 'time-line', should be realistic, proportionate and achievable in line with best practice. this will allow infrastructure and recycling capacity to be built up at a pace that ensures progress with the objectives of the directive whilst not imposing excessive or disproportionate costs. i wish to draw attention to the derogation that sets the same recovery and recycling targets as for the other twelve member states, but allows ireland, greece and portugal longer to achieve them. i urge support for the common position, which sets an accepted deadline of 2012. there is an assumption that all member states should ultimately reach the same recovery and recycling rates, irrespective of size, geography or infrastructure. it is not a question of having done nothing alone. yes, far more could be done, but in ireland's case we have a population of less than four million and too small a market to sustain a packaging manufacturing infrastructure. we import 75% of our packaged goods. there is one paper recycler, little plastics recycling, no metal recyclers and the only glass recycler in the country has recently closed down. therefore we are at a permanent geographical and structural disadvantage. to comply with this directive we must ship packaging waste overseas or build more reprocessing facilities and export the empty packaging, which is uneconomic. the cost will not be proportional to the environmental benefit. i underline what ms jackson said to us, on the commission's recent communication on the thematic strategy on the prevention and recycling of waste, published in may 2003. from an environmental point of view it is more important to optimise collection and recycling in the community as a whole, rather than to consider whether this takes place in a particular member state. this should be reflected in the overall recycling target at community level. in the commissioner's own words, could she please explain how this squares with what we have here today?
mr president, the unanimous sign-off of this emissions trading directive in december 2002 at the council of ministers was a major wake-up call to corporate europe and a signal that this was actually going to happen. quite frankly, i do not think they believed it up to that point. i extend my sincere thanks to the rapporteur, my colleague, mr moreira da silva, for the enormous body of work that he did in bringing all of us to where we are today. ireland has one of the worst records, second only to spain, for greenhouse gas emissions. national emissions allowance capping will ensure that quantifiable kyoto objectives are met and that we decouple economic growth from increased greenhouse gas emissions. national allocations will have to be linearly convergent with the kyoto protocol. the national cap on allowances can start from the 2003 emissions level and not from that of 1990, provided that the allowances are decreased to the kyoto figure by 2012. amendment no 43 is very important as it allows member states to benchmark the best available technology for allowance allocation. this should ensure that one-off, economically-vital industries can be looked after in a member state. the force majeure provision is also necessary until a liquid trading market emerges. it is critical to secure the viability of the emissions trading market in the short term if it is to survive in the longer term. in particular, a situation where, as a result of market design, allowance prices significantly exceeded the long-run marginal cost of abatement within the eu and approached the penalty price would be unsustainable. it is appropriate that provisions be made to deal with unforeseen circumstances during the pilot period of 2005 to 2007. in the absence of market management mechanisms and taking into account the risks involved, the current force majeure clause could provide flexibility for member states to cope with unforeseen events such as market failure, and avoid serious economic shocks. definition by the commission of the circumstances under which it may be applied is appropriate and desirable for member states in advance of them preparing their national allocation plans. in conclusion, the provision for banking 2005 to 2007 surplus allowances into the 2008 to 2012 period effectively reduces the number of allowances available for allocation in that period and will act as a constraint on member states in applying force majeure. nonetheless, given the large uncertainties and the major risks involved, the provision for force majeure must be retained.

hailed as the development round. we all share the belief that priorities should be given to the needs of developing nations. these have not shared the benefits of previous trade rounds and the european union must insist on their full and active participation in the cancun negotiations. market access is a very important element in encouraging integration of developing countries into the world economy. the eu has offered ambitious market openings for developing countries in goods as well as in services, while avoiding the risk of going for total liberalisation, which most developing countries could not cope with at this stage. the 'everything but arms' initiative is evidence of the eu's approach in this regard. i urge the commission to press other developed countries, mr president, i would like to congratulate the president-in-office of the council on his first day and hope his response to us today on the international criminal court is a reflection of his future cooperation with this house. a former nuremberg prosecutor, benjamin b. ferencz, said: 'there can be no peace without justice, no justice without law, no meaningful law without a court to decide what is just and lawful under any given circumstance.' the international criminal court affords us the opportunity to ensure that not only captured prisoners or the lowest of the service people involved in conflicts, but also generals and heads of state can be brought to justice for genocide and for crimes against humanity. it is unfortunate that, while so many positive things happened in the latter half of the twentieth century, words such as 'ethnic cleansing' and 'genocide' have come into our normal vocabulary. we must have a proper mechanism in place to ensure that, if a national court is not able or willing to bring a case against somebody who is accused of crimes against humanity, then there must be an international forum to do so. that is why we ascribe and subscribe to the international criminal court. however, i would hate it if people – especially the people in the gallery watching us today – went away from this chamber thinking that this is merely an opportunity for the european union to bash america. america is wrong in its stance with regard to the international criminal court. however, it is entitled to take that stance; it is entitled to put forward its own viewpoint and its own ideas; it is entitled to make new agreements with third countries, if it so wishes. however, those countries will have to deal with the consequences of those negotiations. finally, we can give leadership, as we already have done, and the best way to do so is by example, not merely by criticising people who do not agree with us.

mr president, the commission has claimed that it is entering a new phase with respect to fisheries agreements and that from now on they are to be called 'partnership agreements'. it is all very well changing what you call them, but if you do not change the approach there is very little to get excited about. the one year extension makes it very clear that not much has changed. i will give you three examples. by the commission's own admission a new protocol was not negotiated because a scientific survey had not been conducted. basing access rights upon scientific information is fundamental to good management, so i do not believe this is very responsible. secondly, vessels are supposed to land fish for the local market, which could be an important factor in food security and yet ship owners can escape this requirement by paying a small fee. in the senegal agreement this requirement is far more constraining so that vessels can lose their licences for failure to comply. thirdly, the by-catch allowed to be kept by the eu fleet is far higher than what the guinean fleet is allowed to keep. for instance, eu cephalopod vessels are allowed to keep over four times as much fish by-catch as guinean vessels. this is clearly discrimination. what has the commission done in its approach to agreements, other than to change the name? this is not an acceptable situation. can the commission tell us if things have improved in the newly-signed protocol, particularly in relation to the fact that ship owners can opt out simply by paying a small fee, which they would be well capable of doing? in relation to discards, this is also completely unacceptable. i would like the commission to give us a few answers on this.
mr president, those who are resisting the notion of increasing the budget in this house should ponder one very stark statistic. up until august 2003, 92 women in ireland were killed over the previous 92 months: one woman per month on average dies in ireland as a result of so-called domestic disputes. that is only the tip of the iceberg, because there are thousands of women and children and young people who are being abused constantly. it behoves us to take this matter seriously. i have no doubt that those who have spoken here regard it as a serious matter. it is important to recognise that daphne has been one of the most successful european projects. it has made a real change to real people's lives in all of the member states. people are alive today who would not be alive if this programme did not exist. i would appeal to the members to bear this in mind when they are voting tomorrow in relation to this question of increasing the budget. i cannot accept that it is impossible for us to find an additional eur 15 million in the vast budget that we will be approving here in a short period of time. it is there: what is missing is the will to search and to find it. finally, i want to make the point that this issue is not the same as the issue of violence between strangers. this is an issue of violence between people who at some point must have loved each other. it is a question of power and how power is abused. we also have to address that in a serious way if we are to get to the root of this problem.
- the agenda calls for the debate on the european convention: presentation of the draft treaty establishing a european constitution. ladies and gentlemen, welcome to this special debate on the european convention. i would like to welcome the president of the convention, mr giscard d'estaing, the president of the commission, mr romano prodi, the deputy prime minister, mr fini, and the minister for foreign affairs, mr frattini, who will be taking part today in this reflection on the work of the convention. this is the first opportunity for us parliamentarians to hear directly from the president of the convention in plenary, about the results of the convention and the progress of its contents up to the intergovernmental conference. i would like to express at the outset the deep admiration and respect which this house has for the work of the convention and for the leadership provided - mainly but not exclusively - by its president, mr valéry giscard d'estaing, who has made an indispensable contribution to the comprehensive and fruitful work of the convention on the future of europe.
president of the convention. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, it is indeed a moment of great emotion for me to be presenting to you, the members of the european parliament, the constitution for europe which the convention has drawn up, a convention which i have had the extraordinary honour of presiding over. as you have just said, mr president, the presentation of the constitution is now taking place because it is the first plenary session of the european parliament following the conclusion of our work. you invited me to come at the beginning of july, but i had not yet presented the text of our work to the council presidency. the presidency of the council had ordered this work and it was therefore to it that we had to hand the text over first. that is why i shall be presenting this text to you during this sitting. i would say that this is your rightful place to do so, because the european parliament is the institution which really drew up our convention and therefore the draft constitution. a long time ago, in 1984, under the brilliant leadership of altiero spinelli, your parliament drew up the first draft of a constitution for europe, at a time when no one dared to speak of it, or even to dream of it. you have had the audacity, the deliberate audacity, to rename your committee on institutional affairs the committee on constitutional affairs from the beginning of the legislature, and i look forward to meeting its chairman, mr napolitano. he's not here yet, we'll see him later. in the wake of the disappointing institutional results of the treaty of nice, you have been calling loudly for a convention. the european council in laeken in december 2001, at the instigation of the belgian prime minister, proved you right. when we have dealt with the substance, your preparatory work in the committee on constitutional affairs, under the chairmanship of mr napolitano, and your reports, which have sometimes preceded and sometimes accompanied our debates, such as the report by alain lamassoure on the central question of the european union's powers, have greatly facilitated our task. i would like to emphasize the outstanding and sympathetic participation of your representatives, of all your representatives, in the work of the convention, and the decisive role played by klaus hänsch and iñigo méndez of vigo - i believe that eighteen months of joint work permit me to call them by their first names - in the deliberations of the convention's presidium. finally, i do not forget, mr president, that it was you who hosted the european convention in your premises. i visited you in july to thank you for your generous hospitality. and as for the benches in your chamber, they were not sure whether they should be considered parliamentary or conventional! this is a moment of emotion, but also of realism, because i am here to present and assess what we have achieved, but also to stress what remains to be done to ensure that europe really has a constitution. when we're trying to evaluate any situation, we often tend to forget where we started. two years ago the very word 'constitution' was still taboo, to the extent that the laeken declaration only indirectly referred to it. today the idea of a constitution for europe has made its breakthrough in public opinion: public opinion is waiting for the constitution. according to the latest eurobarometer survey, which was conducted by the commission in june and july last year, 70% of people in the european union are in favour of a constitution and only 13% are against it. in italy, which holds the presidency of the council and thus has a major responsibility for the outcome of the intergovernmental conference - i take this opportunity to congratulate the vice-president of the council, a member of the convention, and the minister for foreign affairs - the approval of the idea of a constitution is 82%. even in countries that are traditionally more reserved, approval trumps disagreement. i will take the example of finland, whose representatives have been very active in our convention: 53% of the votes were in favour and 37% against. our collective efforts to explain the contents of the constitution have also advanced the understanding of our project by citizens. we have come a long way, it must be admitted, with little publicity and little understanding, but a survey carried out by the commission at the end of june, that is two months ago, shows that 70% of the citizens who have an opinion on our work have a positive opinion of it. and to you, ladies and gentlemen, who represent them, i ask: never forget the citizens. we hear the opinions of many people, leaders, officials, governments, but never forget the citizens: it is for them that we work! during the deliberations of the convention, when i was sitting in your place, mr president, only provisionally, i never stopped thinking about the european man in the street, trying to imagine his reactions to our proposals. what, then, is the result of our work? the draft constitution i present to you is the result of intensive work. as you know, it has been published in all the languages of the union and in the language of each of the new member states. this was done in time to ensure that all citizens throughout the union could have the text in their hands as soon as it was presented to the thessaloniki european council. the conventional ones have been working long and hard. they participated in 26 plenary sessions, some of which were two days long; they heard over 1,800 speeches. all the proposals, amendments and alternative solutions, whether they come from the parties to the conventions, the member states, the european commission, civil society and, of course, the european parliament, have been carefully examined and screened with careful and objective judgment. i therefore say to you frankly that i do not believe that there are any unknown solutions today which have not been explored by the convention. i believe that our proposal goes as far as it is possible to go in the light of the political, social and cultural situation in europe today. far from being, as we have feared at one time or another, the lowest common denominator, it represents, i believe, the overall envelope of what is possible to achieve in the europe of 2003. if we try to go further, which is what some people want, and perhaps i want too, we risk tearing apart a europe that has barely been reunited, either by the refusal of some or the disapproval of others. it's an unacceptable risk that no one has the right to take. and you, the members of the european parliament, have encouraged us to go as far as possible, while drawing the boundaries of what is reasonable and acceptable. what are the essential proposals of the constitution? you identified them as we worked our way through the case. it is not necessary, therefore, to describe them in detail, which would lead to a great deal more time being lost in the debate. i would nevertheless like to stress the fact that many of these were still considered inaccessible, as if out of reach, just two years ago. today they form a strong and cohesive whole. i'll call you back. firstly, a central point around which the whole system is organized: the affirmation of the dual nature of the european union, a union of peoples and a union of european states. secondly, the establishment of a single text replacing all the existing treaties, four plus a few others, and giving the european union legal personality. when i considered, in the spring of 2002, the possibility of having a single text, i looked at the previous work, the research that had been done, and we were faced with obstacles that seemed insurmountable. the second is the incorporation into the constitution of the charter of fundamental rights, which enshrines the rights of citizens. i see mr vitorino, who has given a lot of thought to this subject. another proposal is the clear, transparent and stable definition of the union's competences, three aspects on which i would like to stress. clear definition so that citizens can know these skills and transparent definition so that they are not interpreted within institutions that would have more obscure procedures. the definition of powers is accompanied by the exercise of those powers by means of simple procedures, to which i shall return. the last proposal is the political guarantee of respect for the principle of subsidiarity, involving the national parliaments alongside the european parliament. mr méndez de vigo, who is here, played an important role as chairman of the working party on this subject, which had been in abeyance since 1990. the union also has new means of action in three areas where citizens considered them to be priorities. first of all, justice, because in the area of justice we are planning to create an area of security and justice which will make it possible to combat large-scale crossborder crime more effectively and to ensure mutual recognition of civil rights between the member states. in the field of the union's foreign policy, the second expectation of the citizens is met by the appointment of a european union foreign minister, who will chair the council of foreign ministers and work towards the emergence, if necessary, of a common foreign policy. in the field of common defence, it meets the expectations of the citizens by setting up, among other provisions, a european armaments agency. finally, the economic and social governance of the union will be improved, in particular but not only, between the countries that have adopted the euro to ensure the stability and success of our common european currency. these provisions will mean that the three pillars which have made the management and perception of union acts difficult since the maastricht and amsterdam treaties will disappear from the european landscape. the constitution provides for a single institutional system for europe, i.e. a single institutional system replacing the three-pillar system. the institutions proposed by the constitution are stable, democratic and effective. the european parliament, the first institution of the union in the constitution, becomes the main legislator of the union and the manager of budgetary policy. the european council, now distinguished from the council of ministers because they do not have the same composition or the same powers, provides the impetus for the development of the union and sets its general political priorities. the council will now have a face with a president elected by his peers who will organise its work and keep it in the course of time. the council of ministers will be refocused on the tasks of the legislative and general affairs councils and its various formations will be brought together. the european commission, structured to confirm its collegial character and with a composition adjusted to the number of functions to be exercised, will be the driving force and the main executive of the union. it will express and embody the common european good. the president of the commission may appoint commissioners without voting rights, to ensure, if he so wishes, that all member states are kept informed. i would like to emphasize one essential point in front of you, who have done a great deal of work on this subject: the democratic legitimacy of the system proposed by the constitution. we can no longer speak of a democratic deficit, an expression that was part of the common language of critics of our political system. parliament is the central legislative body in the european system. with a few exceptions - and we have tried to limit them as much as is politically possible - any european law or framework law will have to be voted by you, otherwise it will be rejected. parliament's powers are also extended in budgetary matters. when the constitution comes into force, the president of the commission will be elected by you. there was a difficult debate - i cannot unfortunately go into it - on the question of the possible presentation of the candidates. after long deliberations, in which both the conventional parties and the political groups took part, a common solution was reached. the presentation would be made on the proposal of the european council, but with two new features: on the one hand, taking into account the result of the elections to the parliament and, on the other hand, the holding of the necessary consultations. it is therefore an open proposal. and most importantly, you'll have the right to refuse. if you do not elect, by a majority of your members, the candidate proposed by the european council, the european council will be obliged to propose another within one month. under the leadership of giuliano amato, the convention has done a tremendous job of simplifying and also classifying european decisions. i remember the discussions which took place in your committee on constitutional affairs at the time and the proposals made by jean-louis bourlanges. by distinguishing between legislative and executive acts, we are moving closer to the traditional systems in force in the member states, systems which are familiar and understandable to all citizens. the democratic system devised by montesquieu and the thinkers of the enlightenment - i, like many others, have been very interested in montesquieu's thought - cannot, contrary to what is sometimes said, be transposed because montesquieu's system was a reflection for the needs of a nation state and what he calls the balance of powers is a balance within that nation state. but we have in some way transposed it, to define a new balance of power which takes account of the duality which is and will undoubtedly remain an original feature of the european union: the union of peoples and the union of states. we have therefore defined a democratic model at european level which takes account of the size of the population - 450 million inhabitants - the diversity of the old and new member states, and the desire for unity on the european continent. in short, if i may say so with respect and scrupulousness, we have done montesquieu for europe in the 21st century. (laughter and applause) before it can come into force, there are two major obstacles to overcome: the approval of the constitution by governments and its ratification by the democratic expression of the people, parliaments or referendums. let me say a few words about the role you will have to play in this process. but before i do, i would like to clear up any ambiguity about the future role of the convention. the convention has completed its task. on 20 june 2003, i handed over to the greek presidency, on his behalf, the first two parts of the constitution drawn up by the convention. when i went to rome on 18 july to hand over to the italian presidency the now complete text of the draft constitutional treaty, i added: (i quote this passage in full, which is short, for the reports of your parliament) " the convention has fulfilled the mandate given to it by the laeken european council and has come to an end. by presenting the draft treaty establishing a constitution for europe, the president of the convention considers that he has fulfilled his mission and, consequently, terminates his task. " this means that the convention's role is over and that it is impossible for it to seek to intervene in the proceedings of the intergovernmental conference, since it would have no mandate to do so. on the other hand, the members of the convention, including the president of this house, the vice-presidents and myself, will remain at the disposal of all those, including those in this house, who wish to question us on the arguments which have led us to put forward this or that proposal contained in the constitution. the intergovernmental conference will open in exactly one month's time, under the italian presidency, which may perhaps say something to us shortly. most of the conventionals, before parting, vowed that it would be short and could be completed by the end of this year. the thessaloniki european council decided that the conference would take our draft constitution as a starting point. there are three possible solutions. either the intergovernmental conference improves the draft constitution: it is hard to imagine that it can achieve this, not because of the collective vanity of the authors of our text, but because this conference will run into two obstacles that the convention has managed to avoid: the brevity of time and the rule of unanimity. how can we improve in two and a half months a project which has taken us sixteen months of continuous work to develop? and how can we agree on solutions that go beyond the difficulty of reaching consensus? but let's be good players! if the intergovernmental conference succeeds in improving the constitution, the conventionists will be the first to applaud its success. the second assumption is that the intergovernmental conference will end up with proposals that fall short of those of the convention. in this case, we see the emergence of serious dangers. the reservations or criticisms that we hear expressed here and there about our proposals, particularly on institutional matters, point to a major risk. you can't touch one part of the building without risking shaking the whole thing. those who think they can substantially alter our institutional proposals are, i believe, mistaken. for while they may satisfy some, they may displease and disappoint others. the third solution, which seems preferable, is to approve the draft constitution. (applause) but then it would be a question of approving the draft constitution, which was prepared by the convention, and of course, ladies and gentlemen, the representatives of the presidency would have to make a few amendments to it which were unanimously accepted. i would ask you, without too much insistence, to consider the seriousness of the consequences of failure. because of the season, the place, the sun, the pleasure of meeting you, there is a certain optimism about this meeting. i would ask you to consider the consequences and the seriousness of failure, the disappointment and frustration it would cause to the whole of european public opinion. finally, let us not forget that after the intergovernmental conference the real test will come: the test of ratification in each of the member states, in each of the twenty-five member states. this ratification is far from being acquired in advance. if the draft constitution as drawn up by the convention is submitted to popular ratification, in the form of a referendum by some, and parliamentary approval by others, my personal conviction is that, after an intense effort of explanation and persuasion, this draft will eventually be approved everywhere. if, on the other hand, a mutilated or truncated draft constitution is presented, i fear that it will be rejected in one or more member states. in this case, its defence and support would be deprived of two decisive arguments: consistency and balance, which are combined in the draft constitution. this would open a crisis which europe does not need in the present circumstances and from which it is difficult to imagine how it could emerge. mr president, the european parliament has a major role to play in this whole process and i would ask you to be active and vigilant. you are the one who has to keep the public informed. it will not be an intergovernmental conference of the classic type, that is to say, of the diplomatic type, where experts or diplomats debate among themselves about mutual advantages that some seek to obtain at the expense of others. it will be an intergovernmental conference of a constitutional type, the like of which has never been seen before, which must lead to the emergence of a constitution. it must therefore be subject to special rules. observers from your parliament will be attending this conference. let them alert the public and demand transparency! at the last session of the convention in which you were present, mr president of the council and members of the convention, i suggested that the intergovernmental conference should take as its model our working method, which has been imposed on us, by obliging itself to make public, if necessary on the internet, any proposal for amendment and any amendment to the constitution. (applause) i would like to thank this would therefore enable the public and the press to have a clear idea of the content of the debates. it would also seem to me legitimate that you should be informed at each of your plenary sessions of the progress of the work of the conference, as i have done for the convention with the european council. so you will give an opinion on this intergovernmental conference and you will give it before it opens in rome. it is your responsibility to draft and adopt it, but i think it could be a warning. if the intergovernmental conference were to significantly reduce the scope of the constitutional treaty, which was drawn up in full transparency by the convention and with your extensive contribution, and if it were to be the subject of a negative assessment by the european parliament, it would have little chance of being ratified by the states and the peoples of europe. if, on the other hand, a constitutional treaty close to the convention's draft - we do not expect it to be literally ours - is adopted at the conference by the governments of the union and if it receives the approval of the european parliament, it will occupy a central place in the great political debate of the european elections in june 2004. it will then be an opportunity to call on the vital forces of our continent, to mobilise the interest of civil society and to draw out the undecided from their reserve, because who are these undecided people? it is these who have lost confidence in the union's ability to unite and renew itself. the great debate on the european elections will thus echo the more modest work of our convention, helping europeans to get closer to the union, to understand it better and, finally, to recognise themselves in it. ladies and gentlemen, at the very end of our work, at the request of your representatives, we have added a number of symbols to the constitution, including a motto for the european union: 'united in diversity'. i urge you, i beg you, to help europe to have a constitution which will enable it to live in freedom, peace and happiness, united in its diversity. freedom which is freedom of space, the constitution carefully outlines social goals. you talk about articles on union policy and you say there are clandestine ones. they're not clandestine, but they quickly. in any event, the articles in question are not amended. these are the articles of the treaties, because we had no mandate to amend them except to take account of changes: new institutional system, changes in names, european laws, framework laws, voting procedures, legal basis for policies. but the very description of the policies remains unchanged except for four of them: economic and social governance policy, which is making significant progress even if we could have gone further, the common foreign policy, the common defence policy, and the security and justice policy. mrs frassoni, whom i had met in our debates at the convention, talks about intergovernmental methods. we've removed that term; it is a term that goes back to the very beginning of the convention. we have tried to revive the institutional triangle. there is no intergovernmental body, there are three institutions which work: the parliament which expresses itself, the commission which proposes and manages, and the council of ministers which takes the decisions entrusted to it by the constitution. it is not intergovernmental, it is the taking of community decisions by one of the bodies of the union. you are talking about the european parliament electing the president of the commission. you will see that next time things will be done in accordance with the treaty of nice, that is to say, you will approve and nothing else: your only power will be to approve. under the constitution, you would have to vote to elect and you could refuse the choice that was offered to you. mr pasqua wondered about the transition from technocratic to political. we have tried to go as far as we can in this direction. he questioned our constitutional power. but where are the constituents? mr pasqua, what was the composition of the constitutional committee which drafted the constitution of the fifth republic in the summer of 1958? it was made up of appointed people. in the constituent procedure, what is important is ratification. the constituent is the one who ratifies. in this case, therefore, it will be the european parliament, the referendum in all the countries that can use this procedure - which i hope will be the case in our own - and the national parliament where the constitutional procedure requires it. then i'll close with mr. abitbol. mr abitbol has spoken widely at the convention. so he could see that it was a place of free expression. he was in favor of the convention, so was i, so we both failed. i think that the question will be asked again. the absence of a european political constituency is a mistake. there must be a forum where european political leaders, at both european and national level, can meet on an organized basis. president barón crespo certainly remembers the conference he organized in rome, which was very successful because it was based on this model. mr abitbol is a revolutionary, and there should be one in every assembly. he blames us for making the constitution before the revolution. there are two methods, but we prefer to make a revolution by law. i hope that many of you will be in the next european parliament. if things go as we wish, you will have to debate with a stable president of the european council, who will have to come to you and report on the union's activities after each european council. you will have a union foreign minister to question, and when situations like those you have already experienced arise, there will be an interlocutor to whom you can put your questions: why defend this thesis and not that, why take part in this action and not that? so it will be a revolution by law and in the perspective that was indicated by mr barón crespo: it is montesquieu on a continent-wide scale. the last answer for mr klaus hänsch. i very much appreciated your involvement in the life of the convention, because you were not defending particular interests or lobbies, but were inspired by the common european good. and although we have not always followed your proposals in some respects, as we were looking for solutions of balance and compromise, you have nevertheless inspired many of our advances, particularly in the field of social governance. you have said that if we reopen the discussions we have already had, there is no chance of reaching a balanced compromise. for every amendment that has already been tabled, already discussed and has been accepted in one form or another, or rejected by the convention, what is the use of reopening this debate? you have said it very strongly and i hope you will be heard because, and that is my conclusion, mr president, in the situation we are in, that is to say whether in a few months europe will have a constitution or not, there are actually two approaches. either europe does not get a constitution by reopening the same debates indefinitely, or it gets a constitution by being aware that it will have to be lived with. i therefore do not ask that a revolutionary impulse should come from your assembly, but that it should express the strong will, the very great aspiration of the peoples of europe to move forward on the road to union. mr president, it is a matter of very great concern that the security situation in iraq has deteriorated very badly in recent weeks. the us forces in iraq are simply not able to ensure the security of either iraqis or foreign nationals. sadly, not for the first time in history, a war has been won, but the peace lost. the forces based in iraq are sadly contending with daily acts of sabotage and loss of life. banditry is rife in baghdad and on all major transport routes leading to the capital. the governing council does not appear to command the support of the iraqi people. most iraqis do not see to play the central role in the political, economic and military transition in iraq. we must all seek to restore iraq to the international community under an indigenous and representative government. but the bottom line is that the us and british forces are simply unable to cope with what is a rapidly deteriorating security situation. i am convinced that the difficult political problems in iraq can only be effectively addressed in iraq under the auspices of the united nations. there is growing political support for this position. security issues are always best addressed collectively. the united nations is the body that commands the support and goodwill of the broader international community. i do not believe that the troops in iraq can oversee the peacekeeping efforts in that country. political activities.

mr president, nobody can dispute the need to create a fair global trading system, but we should not delude ourselves in thinking that fully-liberalised trade will in itself bring about fairness. in terms of agricultural policy, for example, abolishing all market support and protection would remove about two-thirds of eu farmers from the land. this is in nobody's interests in either rural or urban areas. the current development round at the wto is supposed to give special attention to the needs of developing countries and their desire to better integrate themselves into the global trading system. this is positive and should, in my view, be fully supported. sixty per cent of the world's population lives in rural areas and the vast majority are in developing countries. it is worth noting, at the same time, that trade in agricultural products represented less than 6% of total global trade in 2000. economic growth, in the initial stages, depends more on developing countries' internal markets than access to markets elsewhere. the experience of agricultural trade liberalisation in mexico should serve as a warning against the promotion of fully open markets as a solution for the needs of developing countries. two decades of this policy in the north american free trade area have led to an increase in rural poverty, malnutrition and emigration. it has also caused increased workloads in agriculture, particularly for women, and an increase in consumer prices. increased profit and market control by multinationals has been at the expense of small family farms. if we add to this lost national revenues and damage to the environment and to biodiversity we see that mexico's experience of seeking to develop its agricultural sector through trade liberalisation has had devastating consequences. in terms of creating a fair trading system, the eu has made a significant contribution with its everything-but-arms initiative. we have committed ourselves to eliminating the customs duties applied to the exports of the world's 48 poorest countries. i should certainly hope that the commission will be forcefully urging other rich countries to follow this lead.
mr president, the next round of world trade talks begins in mexico next week. i have been nominated to act as a negotiator at these talks for the european parliament. i certainly hope that the countries participating in these negotiations – including the european union and the united states of america – come to an agreement on one very sensitive issue. there are 42 million people in the world who are sufferers of the aids virus – many of whom are based in africa – yet the technology and the treatment is available to combat diseases such as aids. if developing countries can be given the right to distribute these much-needed medicines to their own people on their own licensing terms, then the costs of these medicines would be substantially reduced. there is now a growing political will to introduce changes to the international intellectual property rights system so that drugs to combat aids can be given to those countries which do not have the money to pay for them. we all know what our responsibilities are when it comes to the issue of combating aids and we must act accordingly. a successful outcome to these negotiations would mean saving the lives of millions of people in the world. this round of trade talks must truly be a development round. saving people's lives must always come before any doctrine on intellectual property rights.

commission. mr president, the european union policy towards israel lies in partnership and cooperation. it aims to contribute to a resolution of the ongoing conflict, along with other international partners, and in close collaboration with the parties involved. the commission is aware of the difficult circumstances in which the business communities are currently working in the middle east region. at the same time, the european commission, as guardian of the treaty, is responsible for guaranteeing the full and correct application of community law, including international agreements concluded by the community and therefore the implementation of the eu-israel association agreement. i can confirm then that in applying the eu-israel association agreement, the eu relies on international law for the territorial definition of the state of israel, thus excluding the territories under israeli administration since 1967 in the west bank, gaza strip, east jerusalem and the golan heights. therefore, products originating in these areas are not entitled to benefit from preferential treatment under the eu-israel association agreement. following confirmation from israel that its customs authorities certified goods coming from the settlements as being of israeli origin, the commission published a notice to the importers in the official journal of the european union in november 2001, in order to inform them of the situation. according to the provisions of the bilateral agreement, it is the responsibility of the customs administrations of the eu member states to check the origin of goods with the israeli authorities through the post-verification procedure. it is also their responsibility to take the necessary precautions where a customs debt is due. it is in this context that the recovery of duties is now undertaken by the customs administrations of the member states. these measures, initiated by the commission, aim to protect the financial and legal interests of the community. at the same time, i can only reiterate that the commission has always declared its willingness to cooperate and examine any technical proposal from the israeli authorities to find a solution for this issue which would respect the terms of the association agreement. in other words, one can conclude that the commission has taken the necessary measures to ensure correct application of community law. as a result, member states are imposing duties on products from the settlements. we keep this regularly under review with member states' customs authorities and we are also continuing to talk to israel about technical issues related to customs certificates.
mr president, it is a very sensitive time to be discussing an issue like this. firstly, let me put on record my total abhorrence of the terrorist incidents that have happened all too often in the middle east. not only do i condemn the actions of suicide bombers, i also condemn the actions of the security services of the israeli state when they act outside international law, making the resolution of that problem even more intractable. however, some people may feel that this issue should not have been raised because it could complicate the peace process. those of us who have taken the initiative on this particular issue believe that, unfortunately, such an approach has resulted in insufficient action on the part of the commission and member states. the commissioner himself has already outlined the important issues at stake. no one summed up the implications better than commissioner patten himself in a debate in this house in may 2001. it is important to put it on record again, and i quote him: 'the european union's position on settlements is clear: all settlement activities in gaza, the west bank, including east jerusalem, and on the golan heights are illegal, under international law, and constitute a major obstacle to peace. the commission communication (of 1998) made it clear that preferential access to community markets for exports originating in israeli settlements in the west bank and gaza strip and in east jerusalem and the golan heights 'contravenes agreed rules of origin since these territories do not form part of the state of israel under public international law'.' that says it in a nutshell. i listened very carefully to what the commissioner said. the impression we get is very different from what he said in this house today. one does not get the impression that this issue has been pursued vigorously enough by the commission as a whole nor, indeed, by member states. it must be said with regard to israel that at the moment at best it is not being as cooperative as it could be in providing full details on the origin of all products and their component parts to customs authorities. at worst, it could be said that israel is defying its trade agreement with the eu. given the clarity of the comments initially made by commissioner patten, to some extent echoed today, we need to have more assurances that member states are taking sufficient action. therefore, while i welcome what the commissioner has said, i remain unconvinced that this issue has been enforced at a member-state level in the way that it should be.
mr president, the cavalier attitude the israeli authorities display towards their obligations to comply with international law with regard to their trade relations with european union is an indicative example of its attitude to international law in general. the fact that the european union is so weak in exerting its pressure on israel to comply with international law is reflected in the fact that new agreements have been made with israel in recent times. i would like to touch on those. i have enormous respect for the efforts of mr solana, on behalf of the european union, to reduce tension and to encourage a process of peace negotiations, but the european union is undermining his efforts, in my view, by failing to demonstrate its determination to israel that agreements made to israel's commercial and trade advantage must be fully complied with or will be terminated. i have no doubt that the current eu-israel association agreement should be suspended. the actions of the israeli government that deny the palestinians their human rights are in breach of that association agreement. despite repeated calls by myself and others to have a full review of israel's compliance with human rights provisions, nothing tangible has been done, to my knowledge. several months ago the community agreed with israel to expand its preferential import quotas on a number of agricultural products that are largely or mainly produced in its illegal settlements, and these are for export to community markets. the community took this measure without requiring that israel stop violating its agreement by issuing proofs of origin for settlement products. this is not the way to defend or preserve the community's legal right to require the correct implementation of the agreement by israel. the commission is now saying that it will not be possible to include israel in the pan-european cumulation agreement, while israel continues to misapply the origin rules protocol in its existing agreement. the community's political will to maintain this position is not convincing to israel and certainly not convincing to me and many others in this house, while it fails to ensure the correct implementation of the existing agreement. it is my view that the current crisis in the peace process between israel and the palestinians is such that the european union has to exert the greatest possible pressure on the israeli government. in the economic sphere two things need to happen: steps to suspend the association agreement need to be initiated on the basis of breaches of human rights obligations contained in the association agreement; and legal steps should be initiated to recover duties due because israel has misrepresented the origin of its exports. both these steps require the political will of a united commission. i am not convinced that the commission is united on this matter and the consent of the member states is needed. i call upon the irish government to make this a priority for its presidency of the european union. i should like to emphasise that in making these comments i acknowledge that the responsibility to make peace is shared with the palestinian leadership. it must ensure that all possible steps are taken to end the vicious suicide bombings that have caused so much israeli anguish and hardship and have hardened attitudes behind an irresponsible israeli government. likewise the united states must exercise its enormous influence on israel to cease its assassinations and abuses of human rights in the occupied territories. i should like to address two points made by the commissioner. he said that member states are applying duties on settlement goods. my understanding is that only happens in a small number of cases where israel has actually declared these goods to be settlement goods, and it does so only to relieve the pressure of the commission and this house on them in relation to this matter. regarding the post-delivery verification system, once israel declares where the goods come from, there is no way that a member state can legally challenge that verification. i would like the commissioner to address those two issues.
