president of the council. mr president, i thank all the honourable members who have spoken. we have noted all the speeches carefully and will take them into account in the 50 working days that remain before the european council in mid-december. many people have commented on the results and the work of this presidency. i would simply like to point out that it is very difficult - and i have experienced this myself - to deal with all the problems of a presidency when you have a very limited time. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council by the end of the year, and the council will then be able to submit it to the council. in july and august we also tried to meet the heads of state or government, but it was practically impossible and we limited ourselves to bilateral meetings. the actual working time for a presidency in this role in the second half of the year is therefore four months. then there is the christmas period, with the consequent bringing forward of the last european council to 12 and 13 december, and so there is very little time available. this means that we must look with great interest at the proposal contained in the draft constitutional treaty which provides for the establishment of presidencies for two and a half years with the possibility of renewal. i hope that it will be possible to identify an authoritative president who can represent our union with authority on the international stage and who will have the time to carry out perhaps even those revolutions in the systems by which the european council operates, which certainly cannot be done in a time that is too short. i would remind you that during this period the italian presidency has tried to live up to its responsibilities. i would like to ask the president-in-office if he is aware that the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. we have had more than 42 meetings with government representatives from the community and the candidate countries. we have eliminated a number of old disputes which no previous presidency had resolved. we have chaired 26 meetings of ministerial councils, with all the work, including that of the president himself, relating to the preparation of these european councils in the various fields and to the coordination of the councils themselves. we have adopted 17 regulations and directives. we have concluded three conciliation procedures with the european parliament which had been missing for some time. we have concluded or initialled seven international agreements; we have started the technical review of the texts approved by the convention, and this involves numerous meetings, almost always at night, by the president-in-office. we have held eight association and cooperation councils, from armenia to georgia, to jordan, to tunisia and so on. we have held ten summits and troika meetings, and by the way, i am leaving for china this week. we have held 30 coreper meetings, all preparatory meetings; we have had 15 working meetings with representatives of the usa, russia, the balkans, latin america and other countries. we have also held more than 800 meetings of the council's working parties. the future presidency of the european union will therefore have to be highly structured and will have to rely on someone who has the age and strength to cope with such a level of commitment. i am too old for this, mr schulz. thank you, though. (laughter) as for the intergovernmental conference, i recall that it has been open for 18 days. the presidency has initiated a discussion, which was open, albeit brief, and which could not and cannot be prevented. i do not think that it is conceivable that in a body of heads of state or government, each government should be prevented or denied the right to express its own country's position on a constitutional treaty. the task of the presidency has been to listen, to go into each item of discussion and then to summarize it in an overall proposal, which is exactly what we are going to do. the problems which remain, as you know, are mainly institutional. the commission's composition - as has been widely mentioned here - the revision of the constitutional treaty with the possible extension of qualified majority voting. i expect that in a few weeks' time, when we have completed the detailed - but, i repeat, open and transparent - examination of all the issues on the table, we will be able to make an overall proposal. it will be my task to contact the leaders of the various countries bilaterally and then to take it to an informal meeting of the european council, probably between 15 and 30 november, and finally to arrive with the final proposal by mid-december. one thing is certain: europe and its citizens expect a high-quality constitutional treaty. the commission's proposal is to be seen as a success, i.e. as a response to the challenges we will increasingly face. we cannot accept compromises which reduce the european union's capacity to take decisions and to take them quickly and efficiently; we cannot therefore think that the legitimate and understandable defence of individual national interests can prevent a constituent result which is necessary to consolidate the integration of europe, which is enlarging and uniting with an ever-increasing number of new member states. the time will come for a decision in december, when the presidency's overall proposal has been examined, studied and discussed. we shall ask everyone to share in a clear and transparent responsibility for a comprehensive constituent project which, i repeat, must be lofty and noble. i believe that if this were not the case, european citizens would be called upon to vote in june without knowing the new institutions and their confidence in the european union and its progressive integration would be undermined or seriously affected, which is a decisive factor in winning the challenge for a europe capable of playing a leading role on the international scene, capable of competing with dignity on an equal footing with any other international power, capable not only of increasing democracy, freedom, the well-being and security of its citizens but also of spreading these primary goods throughout the world. i think that is something that is worth reflecting on because we have all committed ourselves, once again recently, with the millennium declaration, to give those who still lack them on the planet, food, water, health and education. these are important material goods, but we know very well that unless they are preceded by the first good, the good of freedom, which democracy follows as a form of government, there is no possibility of giving and guaranteeing these goods in a lasting way to the citizens of the world who are still deprived of these goods. i believe that, as we reflect - as i am doing in these days and nights - on the final articles of the constitutional treaty, we should be clear that this treaty will be valid for our fellow citizens for the next ten or twenty years and that it must give our union, as the seat of the oldest civilization, as a consortium of states and citizens who recognize themselves in a common heritage of values, principles, cultures and civilizations, the possibility of being a protagonist in the world, of playing, together with other countries and not in opposition to other countries, a role in exporting to the world the very important good that is freedom and democracy, which alone guarantees the well-being of peoples but which alone can effectively guarantee a future of true peace for the whole world. there are also other more specific issues, some of which have already been answered by mr tajani, such as the european public prosecutor. we will stick to the draft constitutional treaty. as regards the environmental dimension, i would remind you that paragraph 24 of the conclusions includes the environmental dimension in the growth process as an element designed to catalyse innovation and modernisation in key sectors such as energy and transport. i would like to conclude by saying that concrete results have already been achieved, and that this gives hope for the future of the work of the intergovernmental conference. results have been achieved in an area where divisions seemed insurmountable: the european defence sector. it is clear from the work of this european council and will be made concrete in the work of the december council that all the countries of the european union, including the ten new countries that are joining us, are aware that there can be no real european union foreign policy that counts, that is authoritative, if there is not the support of an autonomous european defence force. the system of strengthened or structured cooperation, which allows certain countries with greater military capabilities and the ability and intention to spend on defence to join together, was also accepted, but on three very clear conditions: first, that such cooperation be open at any time to all member states of the european union wishing to participate in it; secondly, the criteria and rules for the operation of such cooperation are not the result of the decision of the states initially establishing such cooperation but are approved by the european council. it will be decided in december whether this approval should be - i hope not - by unanimous vote or by qualified majority vote. the third condition is that european defence must not be seen as an alternative to nato but as a complement to nato itself, which we still regard as one of the pillars that have guaranteed europe more than half a century of peace and security. i can only assure you all that we will be working very hard in these last 50 days and that we will always have a clear idea in mind as far as the constitutional treaty is concerned. we cannot - for the sake of pride and satisfaction - close the intergovernmental conference under the italian presidency. this has never happened in history, because the five intergovernmental conferences that preceded the last one opened under one presidency and always ended under other presidencies. we too, while trying to reach a conclusion and while knowing that the citizens of europe will be called to the polls next spring and that therefore everything possible, indeed more than possible, must be done to make them aware of the roles and the overall context in which the parliament whose members they will be called upon to elect will have to operate, we will never accept to sign a compromise, a constitutional treaty which cannot guarantee europe, and therefore its citizens, to carry out what we all believe should be its function in the years to come. the italian presidency will therefore do everything in its power to conclude the work by december, but it will not allow the work to be concluded on a constitutional text that is a downgrade, that favours the interests of individual states and does not look instead at the common interest of us all, which is precisely the common good. mr president, my group supports the commission's proposals. it has been clear now for many years that cod needs to recover from the excessive pressures put on it by modern-day fishing. like many other species, stocks are far below sustainable levels, and this has led to massive socio-economic problems in coastal communities. people are losing sight of the point here and putting the cart before the horse. the socio-economic problems have arisen from an ecological problem. if you tackle that you are tackling the socio-economic problems, instead of going at it in the opposite direction. there has been over-fishing for many years because of the tacs being set too high, and, basically scientific advice has not been followed. the council has asked for a proposal for a recovery plan, which the commission proposed in 2001, but the council still does not seem to have the courage to adopt it. this is the fourth attempt. the proposal has many good ideas including: outlining conditions under which fishing can be permitted; rules for deciding about fishing, given various levels of stock abundance and also attempts to improve control and surveillance requirements and an initial management of the effort. the ices press release of monday, which mrs stihler has already mentioned, shows that stocks are in grave danger. this is a clear illustration of the danger of setting excessively high quotas, but this has been going on for years and it is still continuing. last year, several tacs were set higher than ices advised. the extreme example is the irish sea, with tacs set on average 28% above scientific advice over the past ten years. is it any wonder that stocks are actually in trouble? ices talks of drawing a line in the sand, but ministers and industry and many of the politicians even seem to be burying their heads in the sands, and this is the problem. ministers actually have to move away from this luddite position of ignoring scientific advice and take the scientific advice on board. it is claimed that the common fisheries policy is getting on to a sustainable basis as a result of the reform of 2002. there have been some advances, such as better provision for control with improved cooperation among member states and the possibility of effort limitation, in addition to classic limits on the amount of fish caught and recognition of the precautionary approach which is essential. but it is not all good. the magps, which we will come back to later today, have disappeared and there is no further requirement for reduction. this all sounds good on paper but it depends entirely on the political will to implement. the commission is making a sincere effort to improve things, and the greens will, as usual, support the commission. however, there is a crucial level for the survival of the stocks. but in the irish sea the commission's proposal would allow fishing below a stock level of 6000 tonnes, whereas ices is now advising closure until stocks reach that level. it is vital that the commission reflects ices advice when recommending tacs for the next year on these stocks. we can no longer ignore ices. mrs stihler has mentioned the situation in canada. that will happen here if we do not take a progressive position.

commission. - the commission would first like to thank mrs mckenna for her report and for the work that has been done on this subject. we generally agree with your analysis, mrs mckenna, of the fleet capacity orientation programmes, what we call pop in our jargon, and in this case pop iv. as you know, we have drawn the consequences of this in the reform of the common fisheries policy to remedy the shortcomings you have mentioned, which have become obvious to everyone. we also share your recommendation that we should no longer finance the export of fishing vessels to third countries: as you know, we suggested this in our reform proposal. the council has deferred its application a little longer than we would have liked, but the main point is that after 2004 exports of fishing vessels with public aid will no longer be possible. however, we do not share your view on the new fleet management tools which were decided upon in the reform of the common fisheries policy: you seem to believe that these new tools will not reduce the overcapacity of the community fleet. i would like to briefly recall the two main advances of this new management policy. the first is the entry and exit regime for fishing vessels - an innovation that has not been welcomed by the profession or the member states - and this regime will be combined with the prohibition on replacing fishing capacity that has been withdrawn with public, national or community funding. this will result in a gradual reduction in our fleet. the second measure is catch limitation schemes. this is obviously an essential part of the plans for the recovery of fish stocks and by limiting catches we will strengthen the efforts to reduce overcapacity. we therefore share your analysis of the shortcomings of the past and believe that the measures adopted in the recent reform of the fisheries policy will make it possible to respond to a very large extent to the concerns you have expressed in your report.
rapporteur. – mr president, this report deals with the commission's review of the multi-annual guidance programmes. technically it covers the period up to 30 june 2002, but since parliament is not going to do a report on the final situation as at 31 december, i will make some comments on the situation up to that date. this was the fourth generation multi-annual guidance programme, a series of programmes dating back to 1983. they tried to exert some control over the size and distribution of eu fleets. they have lasted for 20 years altogether. considering that their objective was to achieve a balance on a sustainable basis between resources and their exploitation, and in the light of the advice coming from ices over the past few days, it can be safely concluded that they have been a resounding failure. to its credit, the commission has proposed a far more comprehensive and important cut in fleet capacity than the council was ever able to accept. for example, the agreed objectives for the member states' combined fleets were so modest that the community fleet as a whole was already smaller than the overall objectives, even before the magp iv entered into force. some fleets required no reductions at all. yet at the end of the programme in december 2002 only five of the 13 countries had met the objectives for all the different fleet segments. spain, often criticised this house, was one of them. clearly the member states did not have their heart in the exercise. now the magps themselves are being scrapped. while we recognise that they were ineffective and cumbersome to administer, at least they had the goal of reducing fleet capacity. what has been put in place in the so-called reform does not even do that. each member state has been allocated a certain capacity for fishing vessels in tonnage and kilowatts, but there is no requirement for that capacity to be reduced. as the commissioner himself said, only if public money is used is there any requirement to reduce capacity. as fish stocks are decreasing in abundance faster than the fishing fleets chasing them, the future does not look bright for either the fish or the coastal communities and the people depending on the fishing industry for a living. this is going to cause a major socio-economic crisis. it is looming on the horizon. as mr stevenson has said, they are going to suffer endless hardship. but that is going to be the case if we do not realise what the problem is and how to address it. as mr lamy is commissioner for trade, he may be interested in knowing how the eu engages in free trade with fishing vessels. during the period 1998 to 2001, at least 746 vessels were exported to third countries. the number could be many times greater but since most of the vessels had left the fleet, the commission has no idea what happened to them. they were simply decommissioned. of those 746 vessels, at least 38 were directly exported to known flag of convenience countries. there are even examples of shipowners being funded by the fifg to export to flag of convenience countries. even mr lamy would have to admit that it is difficult to have a more liberalised trade than that! another problem with the management of the magps by the commission relates to the waters beyond the european union. a couple of years ago, the commission allowed a rather large vessel, the atlantic dawn to join the irish fleet, with the consequence that another vessel, the veronica, was exported to a flag of convenience country, panama. this was supposedly because the fish of mauritania are or were plentiful. earlier this year the commission did a similar favour for the dutch. this time they allowed the equivalent of three 'atlantic dawns' into the dutch register to fish the same fish off dutch. it has now legalised an illegal situation. it sends out a clear signal to anyone else who wants to do this: basically break the law, ignore it, and the commission will help you at the end of the day. that is the wrong signal to send out. it is clear that the commission bends over backwards to accommodate shipowners of these huge supertrawlers. these are not the little coastal communities that will be affected, these are the huge business ventures. i am appalled at commissioner byrne who also bent over backwards to help the owner of the atlantic dawn, the world's biggest pelagic trawler, to get that fishing licence. i believe it was a breach of his duty as a commissioner to act in the interests of an individual businessman from his own country. that should also be investigated. i would like to know how many more commissioners are bending over backwards to facilitate specific business interests against the interests of the community as a whole.

commission - (de) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when we concluded the accession negotiations with the ten candidate countries a year ago, we did so on the assumption that they would be fully prepared by the date set for accession, that is to say, that they would have fulfilled all the obligations which they had to fulfil in the course of the negotiations. that's the reason behind the tracking: it's there to determine whether those predictions were accurate or not. the final follow-up report adopted by the commission yesterday is the last of its kind. two reports have already been prepared, which have had very positive effects. i can tell you that we must of course expect the media, following the debate in this house, to concentrate on the points where we say that the situation still needs to be improved. i therefore think it is necessary to begin by putting these elements back into their context. firstly, we did not have to review most of the acquis communautaire, as it was already clear during the negotiation process that all the requirements had been met. we have not even carried out a second check in this respect. we have only reviewed those areas where issues were left open during the negotiations and where commitments had been incorporated. we have divided this part of the acquis into 140 sectors of very variable importance, some covering several hundred legislative acts, others covering only one - and this is just an illustration of the volume involved. the fact that we had a total of 1,400 such domains to control made the task titanic. this is a collegial effort by the whole commission, involving several hundred staff in recent months, but i would also say that this work is far from negligible and that the overview we have has never been at such a high level in previous enlargements. i must tell you that such work has never been done in the history of the european union, and it is important for us to know this if we are to assess the results of this undertaking correctly. it turned out that in the 1 400 sectors we monitored, preparations were proceeding in full accordance with the timetable in 70% of cases and no comment was needed. in another 27%, we found that some individual issues still needed to be addressed, but that overall the situation was not a cause for concern. this process is under way and we expect everything to be in place by 1 may 2004. so there are 3% - 39 cases out of 1 400, to be exact - where we have observed serious gaps and serious delays which will be difficult to fill. in these cases, we say to the future member states that decisive action must be taken urgently to meet the conditions in time for 1 may 2004, so that everything related to these areas can also be settled. the 39 problem areas are distributed among the ten countries. i would caution against any attempt to establish a ranking: the fact that poland is pinned in ten of these areas does not mean that it is doing less well than the others. this is simply because many of the problems are unique to poland, as the size of other countries means that they are not faced with them. i consider the overall result to be very balanced. it covers only a few chapters of the acquis and we believe that the problems can be solved everywhere even before 1 may 2004. if it is not - and this is crucial - the commission will take the necessary measures in good time before 1 may, and we have a whole range of options. we can apply the security measures which are already contained in the treaty. we can use the specific security measures contained in the accession treaty; we can initiate normal infringement procedures or resort to administrative interventions. we therefore have a wide range of options, and the commission agrees today that each commissioner, within his or her remit, will monitor the management of these outstanding problems and, if necessary, propose the necessary measures in good time before 1 may. i personally do not think we should go that far, because in most cases the negative consequences of these unresolved problems would not affect the community as such, but only the new member states themselves. thus, the question was raised whether the structures allowing for the full allocation of subsidies to agriculture were operational. if the administrative structures are not adapted to this end, the funds will not be released, which will imply considerable internal pressure on the government which is guilty of such negligence, because its farmers will not receive their direct subsidies. so i predict a spontaneous resolution of all these problems by may 1, 2004. as this house is particularly attentive to the question of food safety, i can tell you that there are still some problems in this area and that our position remains unchanged: no food which does not comply with our standards - that is to say, with our health rules - should be allowed to enter the internal market. the necessary food safety measures will therefore be taken by february at the latest to ensure that no non-compliant products enter the internal market. however, the number of such products is relatively limited, and people should not think that a country has performed poorly in a field simply because a few companies in some countries have not met the standards. in summary, we therefore conclude that the institutions and policies will continue to function after 1 may 2004, that no significant bottlenecks should occur and that, while the possibility of problems cannot of course be excluded, they will remain manageable in all respects. all this adds up to a positive result. i wholeheartedly agree with and share the commission's satisfaction in this regard and with the recent remarks by president prodi highlighting the particular achievements of the governments, parliaments and peoples of these countries. in this connection, let me turn to the case of bulgaria, romania and turkey. i'll be relatively brief. bulgaria and romania have made remarkable progress. i would like to stress in particular that bulgaria has finally succeeded in promoting the reform of its judiciary, which was a major problem in previous evaluations. i would like to mention the more positive assessment of romania on the market economy criterion. the commission now says that romania can be considered a market economy, as long as the reform process continues in this way - which we believe it should. this is tantamount to recognising the significant economic reforms romania has already undertaken and the remarkable macroeconomic stability it has demonstrated. as regards the further treatment of romania and bulgaria, the commission recommends that the two processes should not be separated. we are sticking to our objective of integrating both countries simultaneously into the european union in 2007, even if the principle that no country should wait for the other remains in place. so if it turns out during the process that the two countries are progressing at different speeds, we can also conclude the negotiations at different dates. if we can take it as a kind of compliment that both countries are firmly committed to finishing the negotiations before the end of the current commission's mandate, we are very cautious in making a statement on this subject. i would also appreciate it if parliament would follow suit and not specify any date at the moment, but simply confirm the 2007 accession date. to this end, work on the accession treaty will have to be completed before the end of 2005. this means that the negotiations will have to be concluded by the summer of 2005 at the latest, at which time it will be possible to conclude them if the country in question has actually managed to complete all the reforms. overall, i consider this to be a favourable scenario. however, i would once again strongly encourage these countries to make decisive efforts to strengthen political and economic governance. i am referring in particular to the fight against corruption and economic crime. these aspects are also important in fostering the investment climate in these two countries and in making them attractive to investors. we have tried to be unbiased about turkey, and the report the commission has presented today leaves the door open to all speculation about a possible statement on the decision to be taken next year. we have tried not to do that, but rather to give turkey fair and objective treatment, which means that we have to attest and acknowledge that reforms have been implemented better, and at a more sustained pace, in both the political and economic fields - which is remarkable. however, it also means that we must tell the truth and say that there are still many sectors which do not meet our standards or our requirements and that these shortcomings must be remedied. it is foolish to keep silent about either of these aspects. areas, that turkey's willingness to be bound by the decisions of the human rights court remains problematic and, in particular, that major problems are emerging when it comes to implementing the reforms that have been decided. the implementation gap in this area is considerable; the government recognizes that and wants to fix it. president prodi has just referred to the cyprus problem. i must the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. when we concluded negotiations with the 10 acceding countries a year ago, we did so on the basis of a forecast. the forecast was that these 10 countries would be fully ready for accession in time for accession, i.e. that they would have fulfilled all the commitments entered into in the negotiations. that's why we have monitoring, to see if that forecast was correct or not. the final monitoring report adopted by the commission today is the last. we have already had two preliminary reports which have had very positive effects, and, ladies and gentlemen, we must of course expect that after this debate in parliament today the media will concentrate on the points where we say: there is something wrong. i think it is therefore necessary to show the perspective from which this should be seen. firstly, we have not had to review most of the community acquis because it was already clear during the negotiation process that all the requirements were met. we didn't even get a second look at it. we have only looked again at the areas where questions remained open and commitments were made during the negotiations. we have divided this part of the acquis into 140 sectors of very different importance. some of these sectors contain several hundred pieces of legislation, some just one - just to show the volume. it was a huge piece of work. so we had to check a total of 1 400 such sectors. this is a joint effort by the whole commission, involving many, many hundreds of staff over the last few months, but i also claim that this work is very substantial and that we have an overview like we have never had before in previous enlargements. i must tell you that this has never been done before in the history of the union, and it is important to know this in order to be able to assess correctly what has come out of it. in these 1 400 sectors we have examined, it has been found that in 70% of all cases preparations are fully on schedule and no comments are necessary. in another 27% of cases, we found that there are still some things to be done, but there is no reason to worry. this process is under way and our forecast is that everything will be there on 1 may 2004. then there's 3% left. that is precisely 39 cases out of 1 400 in which we have identified serious failures, delays which can only be made up with difficulty. these are the cases in which we say to the future member states: it is absolutely urgent and decisive to take measures to create the conditions before 1 may 2004 so that everything is in order in this area too. the 39 problem areas are spread over 10 countries. i'd advise against trying to rank here. the fact that poland has nine such areas does not mean that poland is worse than others. it is simply because a large part of the problems exist only in poland, because the other countries do not have certain problems because of their size. i think the overall result is very balanced. it also concerns only a few chapters of the acquis and we believe that the problems can be solved before 1 may 2004 everywhere. if not - and this is the crucial point - the commission will take the necessary measures in time before 1 may, and we have a whole range of options. we can apply the security measures already included in the treaty. we can apply the specific security measures provided for in the accession treaty, we can apply normal infringement procedures, we can make administrative interventions. we have a wide range of options, and we have agreed today in the commission that each member of the commission will ensure that these open questions are dealt with and, if necessary, propose the necessary measures in good time before 1 may. i myself do not expect that it will be necessary, because in most cases the problem, if not solved, will have negative consequences only for the new member states, but not for the community as such. the question was, for example, whether the structures were in place to enable the agricultural payments to be made in full. if the administrative structures are not adequate, the result is that the money does not flow, i.e. the government, which is responsible for such a failure, is under considerable pressure at home because its farmers do not receive direct payments. therefore, my forecast is that all these cases will of course be settled before 1 may 2004. i know that the area of food safety is also given special attention here in this house, and that is why i say to you that there are still some problems in some establishments in some countries do not meet the standards, the country as a whole has performed poorly in this area. summing up, we conclude that institutions and policies will continue to mr president, i come to this debate with divided loyalties. on the one hand, there is no doubt that simplifying the existing vehicle tax system to remove obstacles and distortions to the free circulation of passenger cars within the internal market is long overdue. in fact, the prospect of a free market in cars was one of the most talked-about issues dangled tantalisingly in front of our citizens as we embarked on the single market – in ireland, in any case. my country is one of the ten member states with a vehicle registration tax. it is a very high one: i think finland may beat us but we are certainly up there with them. this keeps the prices of passenger cars and all road vehicles amongst the most expensive in the eu, including imports of used cars. we have no indigenous car manufacturing plants, not even assembly plants. our cars are all imported, contributing nothing to employment and adversely affecting our balance of payments. our road network, notwithstanding structural fund generosity over the years, is creaking at the seams and our main towns and cities are gridlocked as our car population has increased dramatically in the last decade or so, and the graph continues relentlessly upwards. in fact, the price of bullocks and the number of new car sales, in no particular order, have long been yardsticks of economic performance in ireland. add to this the fact that our kyoto co2 emissions are now at 1990 levels plus 22% – already 10% over target for 2010, and the fact that there will be little or no decrease in car prices even if there is a removal or reduction in vrt because car manufacturers have had to reduce their prices to offset our high tax regime - and they will revert their prices if the tax burden is lightened - and you have altogether a very complicated field of play. on the other hand, the irish exchequer obtains over eur 800 million annually from vrt, this equates to a 2% increase in the standard rate of income tax and indicates the problems that would ensue if vrt were to be reduced or abolished. if it were to be replaced by additional petrol taxes, an increase of 36 cents per litre would be necessary to make up the difference in tax take. this would be inflationary, as would any commensurate increase in our already high annual circulation tax, resulting in car owners who had already paid vrt on existing vehicles being hit by a double whammy. while i object to paying such high rates of vrt in a so-called single market, i recognise that vrt is a once-off tax capitalised in the value of cars. there is no evidence that the problems with it, such as they are, would warrant a large intrusion into the domestic tax arrangements as contemplated by this commission communication. while i can distinguish between indirect taxes such as vrt and direct taxes such as income and corporation tax, member states are entitled to order their affairs so that motorists contribute to the cost of providing public services, especially to the cost of road and rail construction and the maintenance of our roads. far better that than to increase income tax by 2%. commission involvement in member states' tax arrangements must come with a serious health warning. an ongoing flirtation in this sensitive area is a serious threat to the continued acceptance of the great european project by an increasingly eurosceptic citizenship. i should like to point out to the commissioner that he meddles in the tax affairs of member states at his peril. in conclusion, the future for our single market must lie in a parliamentarians. i hope that our states, too, will equally successfully join the family of member states. in the church of saint pierre-le-jeune in strasbourg there is a fresco depicting the march of nations towards christianity. it depicts a march towards the cross, and the cavalcade of nations is led by germania, which is followed by gallia, italia and anglia. the last in this column of nations integrated into the european union hundreds of years ago. this summer, during the celebrations for our state's 750th anniversary, we unveiled a monument to the first and only king of lithuania, king craftsmen and artisans to come to lithuania from all over europe. throughout the history of lithuania we were fated to go through two occupations, the first lasted for more than the whole of the nineteenth century, while the second covered 50 years of the last century. after world war ii, freedom fighters in lithuania resisted the occupying forces for 12 long years. the struggle, which demanded a huge sacrifice, helped preserve, in the conscience of the people, their aspiration for freedom. during the decisive moments in lithuanian history, our nation has been helped by its ability to mobilise itself. in january 1991 unarmed civilians succeeded in defending the newly-regained independence in the face of a brutal attack by the occupying forces. in spring 2003 90% of those voting responsible member of the european family. our goal is to create a democratic state, and this is enshrined in this strategy for the country's development, approved by parliament. external and internal security of the state and the wellbeing of the citizens are the cornerstones of our membership of the eu. i have been taught a painful lesson over the past few days, but this will only give me additional energy to pursue progress and democracy in lithuania. by no means should successful integration into the euro-atlantic structures be slowed down. our plans to become party to the schengen agreement and european monetary union between 2005 and 2009 may seem ambitious, yet they are an important part of our agenda and they will be implemented. this new stage in the history of lithuania opens up vast possibilities to promote and implement our national interests. i am sure that lithuania is ready to be an effective and reliable partner of other member states. our country has 2.5 million inhabitants, territory twice as big as belgium, and we have the best roads in eastern europe. our greatest asset, however, is the people of lithuania who, regrettably, have been through too much suffering. although world war i was a great blow to lithuania, in the inter-war period we managed, in two decades, to reach a level of economic development that was equal to that of denmark. presently, however, we are a model for the whole of the region. the volume of financial investment is currently growing rapidly. the private sector and free enterprise account for over 80% of gdp which, last year, grew by 7%. our aim is to complete land reform next year. we already have a number of large farms that are working productively. we are a country of rapidly developing advanced technologies. it sector growth in 2002 was as much as 30%. there is no truth, however, that one learns by comparing and i admit that lithuania and other post-communist states are moving towards membership in the european union in the face of a big gap in economic development between 'old' and 'new' europe. this gap has never been as great in previous enlargements and this cannot be masked by declarations or resolutions. this gap is also reflected in the transitional periods that are enshrined in the accession treaties. we take this as a reality but we are not intending to give in to it. our primary goal is to bridge the gap in economic development between the old and new member states. the sooner the new member states catch up with the older ones, the greater the competitiveness of europe will be, and the stronger europe will be. to achieve this without the support of the present member states would take too long and that is why it is a duty for us to use the support promised to us to the best advantage for our people. on the other hand, we must actively take advantage of the benefits of the single market and the four freedoms. we have no transitional periods as far as the freedoms are concerned, with the exception of free movement of labour and i would like to express my thanks to those countries who are going to open up their labour markets to lithuanian citizens in a few months' time. the development of the single market will not be affected if we fail to link up the telecommunications, energy and transport networks. investment in infrastructure is of special importance here. we have made some progress in this area: we have implemented the via baltica project, and that and the power bridge between poland and lithuania have been included in the list of priority projects. this would become an important element in the baltic region's economic development strategy. the decisions on how to develop the baltic sea region must be taken now, and i expect important factor in building lithuania as a welfare state. that is why it is important to provide measures in the european union to bridge not only the economic gap but also the gap in social development. lithuania supports simple and transparent principles for the formation of the eu budget. in the discussion on the new financial perspective, lithuania will seek to ensure that its interests are taken into consideration. we will be responsible for one-fifth of the new external borders of the european union and we also have a neighbour in the form of the kaliningrad region. the same is true about the specific features of lithuania's agriculture. i am sure that, if we use the possibilities of regional cooperation, the region of the baltic sea has a good chance of becoming a centre of a fast-growing economic entity. the new neighbours initiative may also contribute considerably to the development of that region. lithuania will be responsible for one-fifth of the external border of the european union. as head of state i will do my best to ensure that this border is secure and transparently controlled. our experience in dealing with our neighbours will be transferred to the older member states. history tells us that without good neighbours a union cannot be strong. the european union must open up to the countries east of the new borders. it should do so to the extent that these new members are ready to align their legislative frameworks with those of the european union. the greatest achievement of lithuania in the past decade has been to achieve good neighbourly quite a lot has been said about the would-be strategy for the kaliningrad region, it has not yet been prepared. i suggest that we focus on the social and economic development of the kaliningrad precise. we must find solutions to sensitive and open issues and also launch a discussion on issues that were not discussed by the convention. the main challenge faced by the igc is agree on the search for compromise, which is a characteristic feature of the european union, will be particularly important in the enlarged union. it is important that we base our existence on common values, democracy, respect for human dignity and transparency. we must respect each other's culture and identity. all of this will serve to guarantee long-term success for the european union. a reference to mr president, on the subject of commercial arrangements between ryanair and the airport of charleroi in belgium, may i remind the european commission that it tolerated airline monopolies and exorbitant prices for air travel in europe for years. ryanair has helped to reverse air price arrangements in europe; it has secured favourable deals from private airports. surely in this era of competition we should permit public airports to compete with private airports for the generation of air travel business, because at the end of the day it will mean cheaper air prices for consumers. this in turn will send out a positive message from the european union that it is actually supporting measures which promote air travel at a competitive price and help the consumers of europe. before ryanair started to fly to charleroi airport it was a deserted field and now ryanair flies 2 million people in and out, to the satisfaction of consumers using this invaluable air link.

union to parliament. as is the tradition, it is a solemn occasion in the life of our institutions to take stock of the situation and to give an overall view of the activities that the commission intends to carry out in the coming year. sadly, this year we are deeply affected by the tragic events that have been chronicled in these last days. i am thinking of the series of violent actions that sentiments of the whole commission when i offer my condolences to all the women, men and children who have been affected by these tragedies. ladies and gentlemen, the problems we face every day show us that the union is healthy, despite the displeasure of eurosceptics and improvised critics. the situation is not easy, because we are in a delicate and complex transition phase. the prospect of a bigger and stronger union is, however, at hand. we are coming out of two difficult years, but judging by the latest indicators, it seems that the negative phase is now a thing of the past. there is widespread hope that economic activity will pick up in the second half of this year before accelerating in 2004. the worst seems to be over: business and consumer confidence is rising and optimism is somewhat returning among european operators. the recovery is taking place not only in the union but also in other regions of the world. in the united states, monetary and fiscal stimulus and productivity gains are keeping growth rates high. however, there is a strong fear that the deficit will increase further next year due to tax cuts and the costs of the iraq conflict. in japan, the outlook is finally good and the trend in the other asian economies remains positive, with growth estimated at 6.7% next year. positive signals are also coming from the acceding countries: in response to the general recovery in europe and the prospect of enlargement, growth is forecast to be 3.8% next year in these countries. and this proves once again the correctness of the political choices made to encourage unification. however, as i said, the recovery is still fragile and the implementation of the lisbon agenda needs to be accelerated and structural reforms continued. the european initiative for growth, which the commission has been working on since the beginning of the year, has now taken shape. it provides for public and private investment to stimulate growth and employment. with the support of the european council in october, our initial proposal has become a real roadmap with specific actions and timetables to remove the financial and, above all, regulatory and administrative obstacles that are holding back these investments. the initiative also includes a quick-start programme comprising a whole series of projects that are, or will soon be, ready to be launched. in close cooperation with the european investment bank, we have identified 56 projects in the fields of transport networks, energy, telecommunications and research. in drawing up this list, we have applied very clear criteria: firstly, it is work whose projects are at an advanced stage and which can be started immediately; secondly, all projects have a strong cross-border impact; finally, we chose works that can have a multiplier effect on investments - especially private ones - and that have only a small impact on the environment. in addition, in the fields of research and the environment, we have committed ourselves to promoting projects with a strong innovative component. as for financing, total investment - both public and private - will amount to €10 billion per year by 2010. private participation will vary according to the projects. however, as a general rule, we have planned to finance projects 60% from public funds and 40% from private funds. public investment will therefore amount to €6 billion per year, both from the union budget and from national budgets. this is equivalent to about 0.05% of the union's gdp, and you will agree that it is not expensive to give a healthy boost to the european economy. this is a figure that is perfectly compatible with the stability and growth pact. what steps will we take? first, the european council in december will decide whether to approve it. the member states will then implement the administrative and regulatory reforms which are often the real obstacle to this work. this will include the involvement of the private sector. i therefore invite member states to coordinate their national and regional spending programmes with the european initiative in order to maximise the impact of investments. the legislative and work programme for next year coincides, ladies and gentlemen, with major changes for the european union. i will only mention the institutional events: the official entry of 10 new countries on 1 may, the elections in june and the expiry of the commission's mandate on 31 october 2004. the programme i am presenting to you today is intended to complete the achievement of the strategic objectives which the commission has given itself as its mandate. taking into account the particularities of the coming year, it actually includes 73 new proposals; this seems like a lot, but it is significantly less than in previous years. the proposals respond to the political priorities which were discussed in depth with parliament and the council between march and june in the framework of our structured dialogue. the main priority is to shape the future of the enlarged union. it is based on two key points: ensuring the success of accession and preparing the political ground for the new financial perspective. as regards stability, a neighbourhood policy should be established with a view to creating a circle of friendly countries around europe's borders. in addition, the tampere agenda will have to be implemented by 1 may 2004 in order to complete the project of an area of freedom, security and justice. finally, as regards the third priority, growth, the pace of implementation of the lisbon objectives must be accelerated. from an operational point of view, the programme integrates the objectives of the new interinstitutional agreement and aims to simplify legislative activity. for example, we have coordinated our proposals with the union's annual and multiannual programming and we are committed to applying the integrated impact assessment procedure to the most important initiatives. on the subject of stability and security, the commission presented a series of proposals at the thessaloniki summit in the field of justice and home affairs and laid the foundations for a new neighbourhood policy. the proposals on economic issues concern mainly the lisbon strategy, the completion of the internal market, research and, finally, the transeuropean networks. in this context, the recent legislative framework for the chemical sector should not be forgotten. however, it should be noted that this year the workload was very heavy and the commission was not able to complete all its plans. for this reason, the 2004 work programme includes some initiatives which have not yet been implemented. i would like to express the appreciation of the whole college for the very active participation of the european parliament in the programming work. structured dialogue has proved to be a good instrument, but all this can and must be improved. given the deadlines for our two institutions next year, the commission will work closely with parliament to improve our relationship. in particular, we propose that the current dialogue arrangements be replaced by an exchange of views between the conference of presidents of parliamentary committees and mrs de palacio, vice-president of the commission, in april next year; the commission also decided to use the written procedure for the mid-term evaluation of the programme and, finally, to postpone the presentation of the 2005 programme - which will be the responsibility of the next commission - to the december 2004 plenary session, in order to coordinate the timetables. finally, we made a first assessment of the internal reform which has modernised financial and personnel management. the serious irregularities committed in the past in the management of the union's statistical office, eurostat, have prompted us to reflect and to further investigate and to propose an action plan, the guidelines of which i now consider it necessary to present to you. i apologize for the length of my speech, but this is an important part. i had the opportunity to explain this to the conference of presidents on 25 september. i gave my assessment of the facts as they had come to light through the investigations conducted by olaf and the many works carried out by various commission departments. i have nevertheless acknowledged that malfunctions in our communication system, between olaf and the rest of the commission, between the director-general of eurostat and his commissioner, did not allow the commission to take the necessary precautionary measures earlier. i have therefore committed myself to presenting an action plan to remedy this. since my intervention, the internal audit service has completed its report and presented it to the cocobu as part of the 2001 discharge exercise. he does not bring any new facts which would call my analysis into question. in short, there is no doubt that the most serious facts occurred before 1999, that the remedial measures were taken in 2000 and that eurostat, the financial audit and other sources very quickly involved olaf in the main aspects of this case. however, the commission was only able to take action from may 2003 onwards, due to some communication weaknesses at different levels that i identified. we acted with determination; we could have acted sooner, and that is why we are presenting an action plan. this plan is based on the fundamental principles of the reform and important elements include the functional independence of olaf, the new financial regulation, which entered into force in 2003, the new staff statute, the provisions on rights and obligations and the codes of conduct. all these reforms have been introduced gradually. as i said on 25 september, it would therefore be unfair to regard the reform, its successes or its shortcomings, as if everything had been put in place since the year 2000. rather, the period 2000 to 2003 should be considered as a transitional period. the eurostat case illustrates the justification for reforms, in particular the mobility of sensitive functions, the separation of management and control responsibilities and the establishment of an internal auditor. it is therefore a matter of building on the acquis of the reforms we have introduced and which are already bearing fruit. these reforms should be consolidated by strengthening the means available to the political level to assume its political responsibilities. i would like to recall that as far as eurostat itself is concerned, we have taken strong measures since the summer of 2003. the director-general has been replaced, the posts of operational directors have been reopened to publication both inside and outside the institution, the post of director for resources has been changed, the organisation chart has been completely redesigned, etc. finally, the functions of heads of unit have been highly mobile. in this context, it appears necessary, firstly, to revise the code of conduct between commissioners and their departments, which was established in september 1999. while maintaining the general principles underlying the 1999 code, in particular the principle of non-interference in management, greater emphasis should be placed on the political responsibility of the commissioner, which covers not only his own activities but also those of his departments. the revised code of conduct will therefore include a number of provisions to strengthen the commissioner's information so that he can exercise this responsibility in good conditions, i.e. to supervise the work of his departments and give them general instructions, particularly in financial management. the code will also provide for a specific procedure whereby the director-general may refer to the commissioner any facts or developments concerning management which may affect the political responsibility of the commissioner or the college. secondly, i also want to answer another question that the eurostat case has revealed. indeed, in various parts of our institution, some signals, some pieces of information were received on this case before may 2003. taken in isolation, these signals were not such as to make us understand the seriousness of the case. if they had been centralised and analysed as a whole, we would not have had to wait for the first substantive information from olaf to take precautionary measures. i have therefore decided to set up a new mechanism to collect and cross-check all information relating to allegations of fraud, irregularities or wrongdoing, to analyse this information and to inform the commission or the supervisory commissioner, as appropriate, in order to enable them to take any administrative or financial measures, in particular to protect the financial interests of the union. i have decided to personally exercise political supervision of this system with the help of neil kinnock and michaele schreyer. our work will be prepared at the administrative level by a group of officials with the rank of director-general, who will be grouped around the secretary-general. this will in particular enable us to better follow up information received from olaf, idoc and ias. of course, this is not about carrying out additional investigations, nor is it about replacing political or administrative officials, who retain the responsibility for exercising full control over management and for taking appropriate action on information and investigation reports. it is essentially a system of early warning and surveillance. thirdly, i decided to strengthen the information channels between central and operational services, to strengthen the links, to improve practices and to follow up on some of the suggestions mentioned in the internal auditor's report. these are essentially technical measures, but i consider them very important in strengthening the flow of information and checks and balances, measures which i have already presented at cocobu. after my reflection on the eurostat case, i now turn to olaf. everyone agrees that the current situation is not satisfactory in many respects. olaf is a commission department, but it conducts its investigations in complete independence. it is in control of its decisions in the exercise of its operational activity. that is also what we wanted. however, the current legal framework remains unclear as to whether or not information should be provided to the institutions or to investigations. this proved to be detrimental in the case of eurostat. i want to dispel all doubts with this analysis of olaf and confirm my full confidence in mr brüner, its director. i am analysing the organisation of the institution, not criticising the work of its director, who, in the present context, has acted appropriately. the commission is in the difficult position of having to assume politically and legally the action of olaf without having the means to effectively exercise this responsibility, and the commission is also legally responsible for olaf in the event of appeals and, in particular, of possible actions for damages that could be brought by individuals who consider themselves injured. i had proposed to parliament that, in the perspective of a european prosecutor, the full autonomy of olaf should be within a clear political framework. that's always my goal. the continuation of the discussions on the full outsourcing of olaf must remain on our agenda. however, in order to quickly resolve the operational problems that are arising today, i would like to propose an immediate step, which involves an amendment to the olaf regulation with the aim of its adoption by this parliament: we must therefore do something to ensure that our successors have an operational legal framework within which to work in peace. the olaf monitoring committee and the ongoing work in the cocobu, and in particular mr bösch's report on the evaluation of olaf's activities, which will shortly be submitted to your assembly for approval, also underline the need to strengthen the regulatory framework and the commission is taking this into account. i now propose the main improvements envisaged: first, the strengthening of olaf's operational autonomy by re-focusing its activities as necessary, particularly in the context of enlargement. to this end, certain horizontal tasks not related to investigations could usefully be reintegrated into the commission services. secondly, the opportunity for the office to focus on its priorities. to this end, a principle of expediency or discretion should be established and should be included in the regulation. this will enable olaf to refer to the appropriate bodies the follow-up of certain cases of minor importance or not falling within the scope of its priority activities. this will also help to increase the speed and efficiency of investigations. i would point out that any decision to open an investigation or not must remain with olaf. thirdly, the clarification of information flows between olaf, the institutions and bodies concerned will be part of the improvements. this will also require consideration of issues related to the processing of this information by the institution concerned. in particular, a better balance should be struck between protecting the effectiveness of investigations and protecting the financial interests of the union through precautionary measures. this will also require clarification of the question of final responsibility for decisions taken. fourthly, the amendments to the regulation will also cover the essential aspect of the protection of the rights of the defence. fifth, olaf's national public opinions. and it will matter even more to the new european citizens. finally, the effectiveness of the commission does not depend on the number of its members, but on the use it makes of the resources at its disposal. the reforms we have implemented in recent years have already produced good results in this respect. the collegial functioning and the coherence of the commission therefore remain my main concerns. the enlargement of the college is a serious challenge, but we will not solve it by creating a two-tiered commission, with half or almost half of its commissioners reduced to the role of second-in-command. ladies and gentlemen, i have spoken of the short deadlines, but our commission is already looking far ahead. at the beginning of the year we launched a broad reflection on the new financial perspective. in 2007, the union could have 28 member states with about half a billion citizens, and a new constitutional framework. it is therefore clear that we must commission. – the commission considers that addressing developing countries' debt problems is an important means of achieving the community's development cooperation policy objectives. the community is actively participating in the current highly indebted poor countries (hipc) initiative with more than eur 1.6 billion pledged up to now: eur 680 million on its own claims as a creditor and eur 934 million as a donor to the hipc trust fund. the commission would also like to recall that this participation represents much more than the minimum required by the hipc initiative. indeed the community, as a donor, is a major contributor to the hipc trust fund, accounting for almost 25% of the total resources. over and above its expected participation as a creditor, the commission has also earmarked eur 60 million for the settlement of all the special loans that would remain due from least-developed acp countries, after they have benefited from the full application of the hipc terms. it is also worth noting that most of the eu member states have announced their intention to cancel 100% of the bilateral debt, beyond the hipc terms. this means that any further debt cancellation in hipc countries will relate largely to multilateral institutions, non-paris club official creditors and the private sector. at this point in time, it is also clear that the hipc initiative has to be considered as a first important step towards long-term debt sustainability and that it will not be sufficient to ensure the beneficiary countries meet the millennium development goals, especially in countries badly affected by hiv/aids. moreover, the adverse economic effects of hiv/aids are now much more clearly recognised than they were when the hipc initiative was launched, and the commission agrees that it must consider hiv/aids when also discussing long-term debt sustainability. in the framework of the eu-africa dialogue, the issue of africa’s external debt has been part of the agenda since the cairo meeting. the commission has followed up actively the discussions between the chefs de file (france and germany) and the african union representatives. at the latest ministerial troika meeting of the eu-africa dialogue, held in rome on 10 november, which i attended together with the irish foreign minister, it was agreed that discussions and the corresponding report of the issue of africa's external debt should be prepared as a matter of priority and that the experts meeting within the enlarged troika should be held in the first quarter of next year. finally, the commission has recently launched, as an element of the eu-africa dialogue, a study on debt relief beyond the hipc initiative, with the main objective of providing a solid base to assess the situation after the full application of the hipc initiative. this study should provide key elements for shaping, in coordination with member states, the union’s future debt policy. the commission expects to be able to share with parliament the results of this study by early next year. i would add that the complexity of doing something with multilateral debt is much larger and makes anything there much more difficult politically in terms of burden sharing internationally, compared to the handling of bilateral debt. most donor countries that take their responsibility as a donor partner seriously have in fact more or less cancelled all the outstanding bilateral debt. for the commission it is important to note that our share of all this as a creditor is very limited, basically because we are a grant donor and do not lend money to our partners.
the irish government is currently the only eu government currently 100% in favour of the cancellation of the poorest countries' debts. unfortunately, that government does not seem to be very prominent in promoting that policy, even though it was adopted back in july 2002. many people and organisations would like to see this policy promoted during the irish presidency. we would also like the commission to support this. in the uk, the british jubilee debt campaign are trying to mobilise politicians to support this. when we talk in parliament and in the committee on development and cooperation about trying to help developing countries, it has been recognised that cancelling the debt would be one of the most sensible ways of ensuring that we can actually help these countries. the debt is grossly unfair. these countries are being exploited under false pretences. the only way forward for any just society in this day and age should be to promote the policy that the irish government has endorsed. we would like to see that happen during the irish presidency and we would like to see the commission come on board too. commissioner, you have not given any guarantee that you would support this policy. if, for example, we can get the majority of the member states to support this policy and to adopt it, then of course we would like to see the commission support it as well.

mr president, while i appreciate the commission's proposals are an attempt to find best standards and establish common best standards across europe, that will have to be done on the basis of member states agreeing to cooperate in this area. it will require political commitment in many countries going far beyond the current commitment in terms of political will and financial investment in cancer testing and treatment. reports have shown that up to 90% of the people diagnosed with breast cancer can be cured if they are diagnosed early enough. it has been established that up to 100% of cervical cancers can be cured and prevented if proper testing is carried out in the correct age group along with fpv testing. clearly this is an area where huge progress can be made in preventing mortality and also a lot of pain and suffering for the individuals concerned and for their families. it is important to have this debate. i just want to give some statistics on the irish situation specifically, not because i want to criticise the irish government but because, if we are to get cooperation across the board in this area, it is necessary to show how bad the situation is in some countries. for instance, less than 4 000 of the 12 000 patients who require radiotherapy in the republic of ireland each year receive it. public patients face a three-month delay for radiation treatment they have been told is both necessary and urgent. the first five-year analysis of cancer trends in the irish national cancer registry, published in february 2002, showed that 50% of patients with lung cancer received no cancer-specific treatment; 7% of those with leukaemia were not offered chemotherapy; two-thirds of patients in the republic with last-stage stomach cancer received no cancer-specific treatment. regional variations and the availability of radiotherapy have a particular impact on poorer patients, since many cancer sufferers have to travel long distances and stay away from home for long periods. the republic's two radiotherapy units are based in dublin and cork, so, while 39% of patients nationally have radiotherapy for breast cancer, only 24% living in the west of ireland have it. unfortunately things are not getting any better, because funding for those services has been cut. that is the kind of situation we are faced with. i appeal to the house to support the report before us and for the commissioner to make it clear to all member states where these appalling statistics apply that they must get to grips with this issue and save lives.
mr president, i welcome the commission's proposal and the amendments by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy to that proposal, which seeks to improve the existing regulations on the transport of waste, particularly the transnational transport of waste. we recently had the problem of ships sailing from the united states to the uk for dismantling and recovery and when some of them arrived, it was discovered, as we had pointed out here in the european parliament, that there were no facilities in the uk to do the work under european union law. they are now lying there during the winter, to be returned to the united states, creating a further risk to the environment. i welcome the proposals in this report to tighten the definition of waste recovery, to encourage member states to solve the household waste issue self-sufficiently. i would draw attention to the fact that we in the republic of ireland have introduced a 15 cent surcharge on supermarket plastic bags, which has been enormously successful in dramatically reducing the number of plastic bags being issued by supermarkets. this has had a significant impact on the amount of waste. we still have a huge waste problem in ireland. there is huge resistance to incineration because of health fears, unreasonable in my view, but the fears are there. we have to concentrate on reduction and i hope that this new proposal will help to take us in that direction.
mr president, i should also like to thank mr blokland for his report on the proposal before us, which deals with shipments of waste and the various procedures and control regimes they must follow, the requirements of which are to be determined by the type of waste shipped and the type of treatment that would be applied to the waste at its destination. it deals with different levels of control, depending on the risks posed by the waste and its treatment in terms of recovery or disposal. under the proposal, shipments of all waste destined for disposal and shipments of hazardous and semi-hazardous waste destined for recovery will be subject to the requirement of prior written notification and consent. the tacit consent allowed under the current regulation will be abolished. non-hazardous or what is termed 'green list waste for recovery' would remain subject neither to notification nor consent. in other words, the present requirements would remain for green listed waste. there is no doubt that a greater administrative burden will fall on waste companies exporting waste across eu borders and on competent authorities of dispatch. the commission claims that there should be no major economic cost. i would like the commission to tell me specifically whether or not an economic impact analysis was done in relation to this particular proposal, to back-up their claim in relation to the economic costs involved. nevertheless, the harmonisation and tightening up of procedures is generally very welcome from an environmental protection perspective. it is also proposed to clarify the amount and extent of the coverage of the financial guarantee or insurance to be approved by the competent authority of dispatch; all competent authorities are to have access to it and it must also cover possible storage charges. the latter is particularly welcome. the amount of guarantee or insurance is currently the subject of some debate. perhaps the commission could comment on that. it has been generally agreed that a consistent method for calculating this should be developed. the commission has presented a draft outline on how this might be achieved. ireland is a small island nation, effectively without any recovery or incineration facilities. we will be dependent on the orderly shipment of waste for the foreseeable future. i broadly welcome this proposal, but no matter how well-regulated the system is, there will always be risks, culminating in accidents such as the one in april this year, when a german-registered ship, the mulheim, ran aground on the tip of cornwall. it was carrying 2 200 tonnes of shredded car waste from cork in the south-west of ireland to lübeck in germany. mrs jackson gave me a plastic bag of this waste, recovered by the environmental ngos when they were cleaning up the beach in cornwall. that is one of the risks that will always be with us.
